text: Almost every example in the rest of this course is meant to be run and modified interactively, one piece at a time, rather than executed top to bottom as a single script. Jupyter notebooks are the standard tool for that style of work in scientific Python.
Running jupyter notebook opens this dashboard first — a file browser into your project folder, where you open an existing notebook or create a new one.

A notebook is a sequence of cells connected to a single running Python process called the kernel. It mixes two cell types: code cells that run Python and show output directly beneath them, and Markdown cells that render formatted explanatory text. A well-organized notebook alternates between the two, exactly the shape this course's own guides follow.

When you run a code cell, any variables it defines stay alive in the kernel's memory for every other cell to use. The most important thing to internalize: the order cells actually ran in the kernel is not necessarily the order they appear on the page. Each executed cell shows a bracketed execution count recording which numbered run it was, and the real test of correctness is Restart Kernel and Run All, which clears everything and reruns strictly top to bottom.

Magic commands, prefixed with a percent sign, are handled by the notebook environment itself rather than plain Python — percent matplotlib inline shows plots beneath the cell, and percent who lists every variable currently defined in the kernel.
Chapter 2 starts the real linear algebra of this course: why a plain Python list can't do the math a quantum state vector needs, and what NumPy arrays do differently.
